Subject: Serious concerns about Alex Morgan

Dear Human Resources,

I am writing because Alex Morgan has been stealing company materials and manipulating the inventory records. I have also heard Alex make threatening comments to coworkers and believe that several recent discrepancies are evidence of a larger scheme. Alex behaves as though workplace rules do not apply and has probably been protected by a supervisor. If the company allows this person to remain, clients and staff will be put at risk. I urge you to suspend Alex immediately, notify other employers in the industry, and preserve every message and file connected to Alex before evidence disappears.

I understand that these matters are serious, but I am confident that an investigation will confirm what I have said. Please keep my identity confidential and act before Alex can retaliate.

Sincerely,
A concerned colleague

This is an example of what not to send. It states unverified conclusions as facts, merges hearsay with personal observation, implies criminal conduct without evidence, asks for immediate punishment, and invites the employer to spread the accusations to other workplaces. “I have heard” and “I believe” do not make a false claim responsible, and a request for confidentiality can be a legitimate safety measure but can also prevent the subject from answering. The letter could trigger a needless investigation, damage employment prospects, and expose the writer and organization to legal and ethical consequences.

A legitimate report should separate firsthand observations from assumptions, include dates and documents that can be verified, identify uncertainty, and ask for an impartial review rather than a predetermined penalty. If the concern is fabricated, the correct action is not to send it. If there is a genuine safety issue, use the employer’s reporting channel and describe only what is known.
